query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under demanding mechanical loading, a single‐phase high-entropy alloy loses toughness because mechanical stresses promote localized solute diffusion and short-range chemical reordering that precipitate the nucleation of brittle secondary phases (especially along grain boundaries), thereby transforming an initially ductile solid solution into regions susceptible to crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy designed and processed as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with uniformly distributed alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled cyclic mechanical loading (with and without elevated temperature) that mimics service conditions while using in situ microstructural probes (e.g. TEM, microdiffraction) to monitor phase evolution.
generation.conditions: Testing under high strain rates and/or cyclic loading at room and elevated temperatures representative of demanding service environments; comparison to unloaded, as-fabricated baseline specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress-induced localized solute diffusion and short-range ordering leading to formation of brittle secondary phases preferentially at grain boundaries or internal interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical loading enhances atomic mobility in regions of high stress concentration, which results in the departure from a perfectly random solid solution. This localized chemical reordering triggers segregation and the precipitation of phases with lower intrinsic toughness, impairing crack-tip shielding mechanisms and facilitating brittle fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-fabricated baseline, mechanically loaded specimens will display signs of local phase separation (evidenced by emergent secondary phase particles or chemical inhomogeneities) and a measurable drop in fracture toughness. This phase evolution should correlate spatially with sites where cracks initiate and propagate.
generation.baseline: The pristine, single-phase solid solution exhibits high toughness, with uniform deformation via dislocation motion and effective crack blunting mechanisms.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-entropy alloys used in load-bearing applications where service temperatures and/or cyclic mechanical loads are significant; failure is expected under conditions where stress-assisted diffusion becomes appreciable.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of phase segregation and its dependence on specific alloy compositions, loading rates, and temperatures is not yet fully determined. Variations in diffusion kinetics and local chemistry may modulate the onset of embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples from the same single-phase ingot. Subject one set to cyclic mechanical loading (with controlled temperature conditions mimicking service) and keep the other as an unloaded control. Perform in situ (or post-mortem) high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, atom probe tomography) to detect secondary phase formation and solute segregation. Additionally, measure fracture toughness and crack propagation behavior in both sets.
measurements: High-resolution imaging for evidence of secondary phases or chemical reordering along grain boundaries.
Fracture toughness tests to quantify changes in toughness pre- and post-loading.
Mapping of elemental distribution to assess stress-induced segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If mechanically loaded samples do not show any statistically significant formation of distinct secondary phases, localized chemical ordering, or a drop in fracture toughness compared to the baseline (unloaded) samples, then the hypothesis that stress-induced solute diffusion and phase segregation underlie toughness loss is falsified.

Valence electron concentration as key parameter to control the fracture resistance of refractory high-entropy carbides

Abstract: Although high-entropy carbides (HECs) have hardness often superior to that of parent compounds, their brittleness—a problem shared with most ceramics—has severely limited their reliability. Refractory HECs in particular are attracting considerable interest due to their unique combination of mechanical and physical properties, tunable over a vast compositional space. Here, combining statistics of crack formation in bulk specimens subject to mild, moderate, and severe nanoindentation loading with ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of alloys under tension, we show that the resistance to fracture of cubic-B1 HECs correlates with their valence electron concentration (VEC). Electronic structure analyses show that VEC ≳ 9.4 electrons per formula unit enhances alloy fracture resistance due to a facile rehybridization of electronic metallic states, which activates transformation plasticity at the yield point. Superhard bulk high-entropy carbides with enhanced toughness via metastable in-situ particles

Abstract: Despite the extremely high hardness of recently proposed high-entropy carbides (HECs), the low fracture toughness limits their applications in harsh mechanical environment. Here, we introduce a metastability engineering strategy to achieve superhard HECs with enhanced toughness via in-situ metastable particles. This is realized by developing a (WTaNbZrTi)C HEC showing a solid solution matrix with uniformly dispersed in-situ tetragonal and monoclinic ZrO2 particles. Apart from a high hardness of 21.0 GPa, the HEC can obtain an enhanced fracture toughness of 5.89 MPa·m1/2, significantly exceeding the value predicted by rule of mixture and that of other reported HECs. The toughening effect is primarily attributed to the transformation of the metastable tetragonal ZrO2 particles under mechanical loading, which promotes crack tip shielding mechanisms including crack deflection, crack bridging and crack branching. A strong fracture-resistant high-entropy alloy with nano-bridged honeycomb microstructure intrinsically toughened by 3D-printing

Abstract: Strengthening materials via conventional “top-down” processes generally involves restricting dislocation movement by precipitation or grain refinement, which invariably restricts the movement of dislocations away from, or towards, a crack tip, thereby severely compromising their fracture resistance. In the present study, a high-entropy alloy Al0.5CrCoFeNi is produced by the laser powder-bed fusion process, a “bottom-up” additive manufacturing process similar to how nature builds structures, with the microstructure resembling a nano-bridged honeycomb structure consisting of a face-centered cubic (fcc) matrix and an interwoven hexagonal net of an ordered body-centered cubic B2 phase. Temperature dependence of elastic and plastic deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy

Abstract: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results.
